core: Working definition of research literacy: the ability to find, read, and judge health research (built from NLM/MedlinePlus evaluation guidance and NIH's description of how clinical research works)
Why nurses need it: care decisions lean on evidence; nurses choose, explain, and defend care
Four study types named, each with one line: randomized trial (clinical trial), cohort study, case-control study, systematic review
Four parts of a study, each named with one line: question, methods, results, limitations
Four questions to ask: Who was studied? How big? Compared to what? Who paid?
Bias and chance as the two ways studies mislead, stated simply with original examples
The honest framing: research literacy is asking better questions, not memorizing statistics
supporting: Randomization and blinding as bias-reduction techniques in trials (NIH)
Statistical significance as the relative chance that results are reliable (OpenStax)
The hierarchy of evidence as a classification of studies by strength (OpenStax)
Sponsor funding of clinical trials and the MedlinePlus caution about business-funded information
outOfScope: Evidence-based practice process and the EBP triad (owned by the evidence-based-practice sibling topic)
Clinical judgment models and decision-making theory (owned by the clinical-judgment-foundations sibling topic)
Statistics depth, p-values, effect sizes, and study-design mechanics (owned by the research-methods subject)
How to conduct research or design studies

claims.claim: Research literacy is the ability to find, read, and judge health research. The judging half follows the National Library of Medicine's guidance that health information should be evaluated by asking who runs the site, who pays for it, and whether it is balanced and based on research, and NIH's explanation of how clinical research is designed and reported.

Nurses need research literacy because care decisions lean on evidence: NIH describes clinical research as medical research that involves people and clinical trials as the studies at the heart of medical advances, the way we learn whether drugs, devices, or procedures are safe and effective.

A randomized trial (clinical trial) is experimental: the investigator determines exposure through a controlled process — for example, randomly assigning some participants to a new vaccine and others to a placebo — and then tracks and compares the groups (CDC).

A cohort study records whether each participant is exposed or not and then tracks participants to see who develops the outcome of interest; a case-control study starts by enrolling people with the disease and a comparison group without it, then compares past exposures between the groups (CDC).

A systematic review gathers all the research articles written on a given topic and often evaluates individual articles for quality; the hierarchy of evidence classifies studies by type as one way to judge the strength of research (OpenStax).

A research article is built from identifiable parts: the question the study aims to answer, the methods section describing how the study was conducted (patient population, setting, variables, data analysis), the results section describing what was learned from the data, and the discussion, which includes the study's limitations (OpenStax).

Bias is a systematic slant in how a study is designed, run, or interpreted; randomization (assignment by chance rather than by choice) and blinding (keeping participants and research teams from knowing who got what) are used to avoid or reduce bias (NIH).

Chance can make a result look real when it is not; statistical significance describes the relative chance that results are reliable and would be reproducible with a different group of similar patients (OpenStax).

Who paid for research matters to readers: MedlinePlus advises asking who pays for a website and warns that if a business pays for the site, the health information may favor that business and its products; NIH notes that the sponsor of a clinical trial is responsible for initiating, managing, or financing it.

Research literacy is asking better questions rather than memorizing statistics: the reader's questions (who was studied, how big, compared to what, who paid) give leverage on study strength without computing statistics.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The term 'research literacy' has no single canonical definition in the Tier A/B sources; sources define the component skills (evaluating health information, understanding clinical research) rather than the compound term.
positions: MedlinePlus defines the evaluation half: ask who runs the site, who pays, and whether the information is balanced and based on research.
NIH defines the reading half: how clinical research is designed, run, and reported (protocols, randomization, blinding, sponsors).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states its working definition — the ability to find, read, and judge health research — as a synthesis built from the NLM/MedlinePlus and NIH descriptions, and attributes those sources in the text rather than presenting the definition as a quotation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources name and classify study types with slightly different vocabulary (e.g., 'randomized trial' vs. 'clinical trial' vs. 'experimental study'; OpenStax also lists narrative reviews and meta-reviews alongside systematic reviews).
positions: CDC classifies studies as experimental (clinical trials) or observational (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional).
OpenStax presents the evidence hierarchy with systematic reviews and meta-reviews near the top and describes experimental research as testing an intervention's effect.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches four one-line descriptions (randomized trial, cohort, case-control, systematic review) that are consistent across CDC and OpenStax, and explicitly leaves study-design depth to the research-methods subject.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate claims (that 'college courses use research literacy as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions' and that the concept is 'a label on a toolbox drawer') were generic placeholders with no source support and were discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate lesson (no substantive content) with a fully source-verified lesson on the working definition, why nurses need research literacy, the four study types, the four parts of a study, the four reader's questions, bias and chance, and the honest framing.

sourceRecords.title: NIH Clinical Research Trials and You — The Basics
sourceRecords.provider: National Institutes of Health (NIH), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: clinical research as medical research that involves people; clinical trials as the studies at the heart of medical advances that look at new ways to prevent, detect, or treat disease; randomization as assignment of treatments by chance rather than by choice, done to avoid bias in assigning volunteers; blinding/masking to prevent research team members and participants from influencing results and to reduce bias; the protocol as the study plan describing the goal, who is eligible, and what information will be gathered; the sponsor as the party responsible for initiating, managing, or financing the trial; informed consent and IRB review. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice (SS1978), Lesson 1, Section 7: Analytic Epidemiology
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. cdc.gov blocks direct fetch (HTTP 403); read via Internet Archive capture of 2020-04-06 (timestamp 20200406175433) of the canonical URL. Supports: epidemiologic studies fall into two categories, experimental and observational; in an experimental study (clinical trial) the investigator determines exposure through a controlled process, e.g., randomly assigning some participants to a new vaccine and others to a placebo, then tracking and comparing the groups; in an observational study the epidemiologist observes exposure and disease status; the two most common observational types are cohort studies (records whether each participant is exposed or not, then tracks participants to see who develops the disease of interest) and case-control studies (starts by enrolling people with disease, enrolls a comparison group without disease, then compares previous exposures between the two groups). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Fundamentals of Nursing, Section 15.1: Evidence-Based Research
sourceRecords.notes: Reused from the phase-4 source registry (identical id and URL). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: the research question(s) the study aims to answer appear in the article introduction; the methods section provides details about how the study was conducted, including the patient population, setting, variables, and how data were analyzed; the results section describes what was learned from analyzing the data, including statistical analyses; the discussion/conclusion includes the study's limitations; statistical significance describes the relative chance that results are reliable and would be reproducible with a different group of similar patients; systematic reviews systematically retrieve all research articles on a given topic and often evaluate individual articles for quality; the hierarchy of evidence classifies evidence into categories by the type of research represented as one way to evaluate the strength of research; an experimental research approach studies the effect of a new intervention and evaluates its effectiveness. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Evaluating Health Information
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: Reused from the phase-4 source registry (identical id and URL). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: health information from media and the Internet is not all trustworthy, so it is important to evaluate it; questions to ask include who runs the site, whether the owners can be trusted to provide balanced accurate information, who pays for the site (ads should be clearly marked; if a business pays for the site, the health information may favor that business and its products), and whether the information is high quality — balanced facts based on research rather than promotion of one treatment; good health information is typically found on sites run by federal government agencies, medical schools, and large professional or nonprofit organizations. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
